parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Radioactive decay is a spontaneous process.

State the meaning, in this context, of the term spontaneous.

markscheme_points.text: (decay is) not affected by external / environmental factors

hints: Hint 1: Think about whether changing temperature, pressure or chemical environment outside the nucleus can make a particular nucleus decay sooner or later.
parts.proper_answer: Spontaneous means the decay is not affected by any external / environmental factors and cannot be controlled.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What spontaneous really means**
Think of the nucleus as isolated from the everyday world. Heating it, cooling it, squeezing it or joining it to other atoms in a molecule makes no difference to when it will decay. That is very different from a chemical reaction, which you can speed up by heating.

Step 2: **Examiner-standard line**
So you can simply say the probability of decay per unit time is unaffected by external factors. It happens randomly on its own, without any outside trigger.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Two radioactive isotopes $X$ and $Y$ each decay to form a stable isotope.
A sample initially contains only atoms of isotope $X$. At this time, its activity is $4A$.
Another sample initially contains only atoms of $Y$. At this time, its activity is $A$.

Fig. 10.1 shows the variation of the activity of each sample with time $t$ between $t = 0$ and $t = 6T$.

{{figure:figure_10_1}}

Fig. 10.1

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
Complete Table 10.1 to give expressions, in terms of either or both of $A$ and $T$, for the quantities indicated for each of the samples.

Table 10.1

markscheme_points.text: half-life of X = 2T and half-life of Y = 3T
both samples show decay constant, in terms of 1 / T, equal to ln 2 / half-life (decay constant of X = ln 2 / 2T and decay constant of Y = ln 2 / 3T if both half-lives correct)

both samples show N0, in terms of AT, equal to initial activity / decay constant (N0 for X = 8AT / ln 2 and N0 for Y = 3AT / ln 2 if both decay constants correct) (Fully correct table: | | half-life | decay constant | A0 | N0 | | X | 2T | ln 2 / 2T | 4A | 8AT / ln 2 | | Y | 3T | ln 2 / 3T | A | 3AT / ln 2 |)

hints: Hint 1: Read the half-life straight from Fig. 10.1 by finding the time for activity to fall to half its starting value - for X from $4A$ to $2A$, for Y from $A$ to $A/2$.
Hint 2: Recall how decay constant $\lambda$ is linked to half-life, $\lambda = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$, and write each $\lambda$ in terms of $1/T$.
Hint 3: Use $A_0 = \lambda N_0$ at $t=0$ to get $N_0 = A_0/\lambda$ and substitute your $A_0$ and $\lambda$ values to leave an expression in $A$ and $T$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read half-lives from the graph**
Half-life is the time for activity to halve. For X, $A_0 = 4A$. It falls to $2A$ at $t = 2T$, so $t_{1/2,X} = 2T$. For Y, $A_0 = A$. Follow its curve: it falls to $A/2$ at $t = 3T$, so $t_{1/2,Y} = 3T$. This is the key first step - do not try to calculate, just read.

Step 2: **Get the decay constants**
You know $$ \lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} $$ So: $$ \lambda_X = \frac{\ln 2}{2T} $$ $$ \lambda_Y = \frac{\ln 2}{3T} $$ A larger half-life means a smaller decay constant, which makes sense because Y decays more slowly.

Step 3: **Get the initial numbers of nuclei**
At any time $A = \lambda N$, so at $t=0$, $N_0 = A_0/\lambda$. For X: $$ N_{0,X} = \frac{4A}{\ln 2 / 2T} = \frac{8AT}{\ln 2} $$ For Y: $$ N_{0,Y} = \frac{A}{\ln 2 / 3T} = \frac{3AT}{\ln 2} $$ Note X starts with more nuclei and also decays faster, giving it the much larger initial activity.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine, in terms of $T$, the time at which the two samples will have equal activities.

markscheme_points.text: correct substitution of A0 and λ into A0 exp (−λt) for sample X or sample Y

hints: Hint 1: Start by writing the activity decay law $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ separately for X and Y using the $A_0$ and $\lambda$ values from (b)(i).
Hint 2: Set the two expressions equal for the time when activities match, so $4A$ times its exponential equals $A$ times its exponential.
Hint 3: Cancel $A$ and solve the exponential equation by taking natural logs or comparing powers, remembering $4 = 2^2 = e^{2\ln 2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write both decay equations**
The law is $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. Using part (i): $$ A_X = 4A \exp\left(-\frac{\ln 2}{2T}t\right) $$ $$ A_Y = A \exp\left(-\frac{\ln 2}{3T}t\right) $$ You are looking for $t$ where $A_X = A_Y$.

Step 2: **Equate and simplify**
Set them equal: $$ 4A \exp\left(-\frac{t \ln 2}{2T}\right) = A \exp\left(-\frac{t \ln 2}{3T}\right) $$ Cancel $A$: $$ 4 \exp\left(-\frac{t \ln 2}{2T}\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{t \ln 2}{3T}\right) $$

Step 3: **Solve for t**
Take natural log of both sides. Since $\ln 4 = 2\ln 2$: $$ \ln 4 - \frac{t \ln 2}{2T} = -\frac{t \ln 2}{3T} $$ $$ 2\ln 2 = \frac{t \ln 2}{2T} - \frac{t \ln 2}{3T} = \frac{t \ln 2}{6T} $$ Cancel $\ln 2$: $$ 2 = \frac{t}{6T} $$ $$ t = 12T $$ This is beyond $6T$ on the graph, which is why the curves have not yet crossed in Fig. 10.1 - X starts higher but decays faster, so Y eventually catches up.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A radiation detector is placed near to one of the samples in (b).

Explain why the count rate measured by the detector is less than the activity of the sample.

markscheme_points.text: Any two points from: • (radiation) emitted in all directions, not just in direction of detector • some radiation absorbed by air / sample / window of detector • some radiation may not register even though it reaches detector

hints: Hint 1: Think about the direction the radiation leaves the sample - does all of it travel toward the small detector?
Hint 2: Think about what can happen to the radiation between leaving a nucleus and being recorded, even if it is heading toward the detector.
parts.proper_answer: Radiation is emitted in all directions so only a fraction reaches the detector. Some is absorbed in air / sample / detector window and some reaching the detector is not registered. So count rate < activity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Activity is not the same as count rate**
Activity is the total number of decays per second in the whole sample, in all directions. Count rate is only the number of decays your detector actually records per second.

Step 2: **Why so many are missed**
First, emission is isotropic - radiation goes out in all directions, but your detector only covers a small solid angle, so most particles or photons miss it completely. Second, even those heading the right way may be absorbed by the sample itself, by air, or by the detector window. Third, the detector is not 100% efficient - some radiation entering it still fails to produce a count. All three effects make measured count rate much less than true activity.
